title: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
summary: Keep a structured filters object across a search conversation: add, replace, remove and reset slots, resolve the second one and those, decide when to ask, store state, and measure it with joint goal accuracy.
outcomes: Explain why last-message, append-only and transcript-concatenation designs lose or resurrect constraints across turns.
Represent search state as a fixed filters schema and map each turn to add, replace, remove, reset or carryover per slot.
Emit state diffs with schema-constrained function calling and build the query from the state in code.
Resolve ordinal, attribute and set references against a stored list of shown results, and decide when to ask a clarifying question.
Compute joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy for a session and explain why slot accuracy overstates quality.

lessons.title: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state

blocks.md:
A job seeker types five messages into a search assistant:

1. Senior backend engineer jobs in the US, at least 150k
2. now only remote ones
3. actually make it staff level
4. drop the salary limit
5. start over: data engineer roles in Canada

Only the first message is a complete search. Every later message is an **edit** to the search that is already running: it adds a constraint, changes one, deletes one, or throws everything away.

The prerequisite course rewrote a follow-up like *How does it elect a leader?* (after *What is Raft?*) into a standalone query that names Raft. That works when the query is a question. In filtered search the query is mostly a **set of constraints** (role, level, location, remote, minimum salary), and the user manages that set across turns. This course treats the set as an explicit, structured object, the **search state**, and updates it every turn.

Three designs that do not keep explicit state, and how each one breaks:

- **Last message only.** Search with whatever the latest message says. *now only remote ones* forgets role, level, location and salary.
- **Append only.** Accumulate every constraint ever mentioned. *drop the salary limit* has nothing to append, so the limit silently stays.
- **Concatenate the transcript.** Hand the whole chat to the retriever as text. Deleted constraints are still in the text, so a deletion looks the same as a mention.

blocks.title: Matching jobs per turn in a 12-posting toy index

scenes.caption: Correct state tracking: 2, 1, 2, 3, 2 matches. Removing the salary limit at T4 lets the 135k staff job back in, so the count rises from 2 to 3.
Last message only: T2 searches just remote=true and returns 9 jobs of every role. T4 has no constraint at all and returns all 12. Every constraint the user built is lost.
Append only: identical until T4, where the salary limit is never removed. The user asked for more results and sees the same 2. Nothing errors; the system just ignores the request.

blocks.prompt: Under the append-only design, the user says *drop the salary limit* at T4 and the result count stays at 2. What will a typical user conclude, and what will your logs show?
blocks.reveal: The user concludes the assistant did not understand and either repeats themselves or leaves. Your logs show a successful query with results and no error, so the failure is invisible unless you evaluate the **state** itself. Silent wrong state is the main failure mode of conversational search, which is why lesson 6 measures state accuracy directly.

blocks.md: The research record agrees that context errors compound. In TREC CAsT 2019 (the TREC Conversational Assistance Track), automatic systems fell from about 0.30 mean NDCG@3 at the first turn to about 0.23 by turn eight, a statistically significant 23% drop, while runs given manually resolved utterances ended statistically level with their first turn. The best manual run beat the best automatic one by about 35%. Understanding the conversation, not ranking, was the bottleneck.

Zamani et al.'s survey *Conversational Information Seeking* draws the line this course uses. Task-oriented dialogue systems keep an explicit **frame**: a schema of typed slots and their values, updated by a task called **dialogue state tracking (DST)**. Open-domain conversational search usually has no such schema and relies on query rewriting instead. Job, product, flight and real-estate search all have a filter schema, so they sit on the task-oriented side, and the DST literature is the right toolbox.

blocks.title: One turn of a stateful search assistant

scenes.caption: The tracker reads the new message together with the previous state, not just the message. Context lives in the state.
The tracker outputs a small diff (remove salary_min). Plain code applies it, so the update rules are deterministic and testable.
The query is built from the state, never from the raw chat text. The same state always produces the same query.
The ids of the results the user actually saw are saved too, so the next turn can resolve *the second one* (lesson 4).

blocks.md: The state object, not the transcript, is the source of truth for what the user wants right now. The LLM proposes changes to it; code applies them; the query is a pure function of it.

Misconception: a good standalone rewrite makes state unnecessary. To handle *drop the salary limit*, the rewrite must restate every surviving constraint as text, and the search engine must parse those constraints back into filters. That is two lossy conversions per turn, and a deleted constraint can come back if either one slips.

blocks.question: At T2 (*now only remote ones*) the last-message-only design returns 9 jobs. Why is this worse than returning zero?
options: Because 9 results are slower to rank than 0
Because the results look plausible, so the user may not notice that role, level, location and salary were all dropped
Because remote=true is an invalid filter on its own
It is not worse; more results always help recall
blocks.explain: Zero results signals a problem; 9 remote jobs of mixed roles look like an answer. Silent, plausible errors are the costly ones in conversational search, because neither the user nor the logs flag them.

blocks.question: Which product is the best fit for explicit slot-based state tracking rather than pure query rewriting?
options: A job search with filters for role, level, location, remote and salary
An open-domain assistant answering follow-up questions about history
A chatbot that summarizes a single uploaded PDF
A spell checker
blocks.explain: Slot-based tracking needs a schema of constraints. The job search has one, which puts it on the task-oriented side of the line the CIS survey draws. Open-domain QA has no fixed schema and usually relies on rewriting.

lessons.title: The filters object and its four update operations

blocks.md: In DST, the **dialogue state** (also called the belief state) is the set of slot-value pairs that describe the user's goal so far. MultiWOZ, a dataset of about 10,000 human-human dialogues released by Budzianowski et al. in 2018, labels this state at every turn. Each slot is a domain plus a name, such as *hotel-area*. TRADE's five-domain setup has 30 such slots and over 4,500 possible values.

For search, the state is a **filters object** with a fixed schema. Every slot is always present; a slot the user has not constrained holds `null`. Keeping all keys present makes diffs, comparisons and evaluation simple.

blocks.caption: The state after T1. remote is null: the user has said nothing about it, so no filter is applied.

blocks.md: DST models distinguish two special values. **null** (TRADE calls it *none*) means the slot has not been mentioned. **dontcare** means the user said explicitly that any value is fine. TRADE's slot gate is a three-way classifier per slot over *ptr* (copy a value from the dialogue), *none* and *dontcare*. SOM-DST (Kim et al., 2020) goes one step further and predicts an **operation** per slot each turn: CARRYOVER, DELETE, DONTCARE or UPDATE.

blocks.caption: SOM-DST's update rule for slot j at turn t. Only UPDATE needs a generated value; the other three are cheap.

blocks.md:
Product teams usually name four user-facing operations. They map onto the SOM-DST set:

- **add**: a null slot gets a value (*now only remote ones*). UPDATE.
- **replace**: a slot changes value (*make it staff level*). UPDATE.
- **remove**: a slot goes back to null (*drop the salary limit*). DELETE.
- **reset**: every slot goes to null, then new values are added (*start over*). DELETE on every filled slot, then UPDATE.

Every slot not touched is carried over. Carryover is the default, not something the model must decide to do.

scenes.caption: Add: an unconstrained slot gets its first value. *now only remote ones* moves remote from null to true.
Replace: the slot already has a value and the user names another. *make it staff level* moves level from senior to staff. Old and new are both values, so this is an UPDATE.
Remove: the user deletes a constraint. The slot returns to null and the filter disappears from the query.
Dontcare: the user says any value is fine (*any level works*). For filtering it behaves like null, but it also records that the question was answered, so the system should not ask about it again.
Reset: every slot returns to null in one step, then the new message's values are added. Without it, old slots leak into the new search.

blocks.prompt: SOM-DST reports how often each operation occurs per slot per turn on the MultiWOZ 2.1 test set. Guess the order from most to least frequent, and guess which one the model is worst at.
blocks.reveal: CARRYOVER dominates (212,297 slot-turns, 96.04%), then UPDATE (8,399, 3.80%), DONTCARE (235, 0.11%) and DELETE (109, 0.05%). The test F1 follows the same order: 98.66, 80.10, 32.51 and **2.86** for DELETE. The rare operations are the ones models barely learn, and they are exactly the turns like *drop the salary limit*.

scenes.caption: Share of all 221,040 slot-turn operations (percent). Almost every slot on almost every turn is simply carried over.
Test F1 per operation (from SOM-DST Table 5). DELETE scores 2.86: a tracker trained on this data almost never gets a deletion right.

blocks.md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

One more schema decision: is a slot **single-valued** or **multi-valued**? If location is a list, *also Canada* adds to it and *Canada instead* replaces it. If it is single-valued, both replace. Decide this per slot in the schema, because the tracker cannot guess it, and the same words produce different states under the two choices.
Model the state as a fixed schema where every slot is present and null means unconstrained. Each turn applies one of a few explicit operations per slot, and carryover is the default.

blocks.question: The user says *any seniority is fine*. Which state change is most faithful to what they said?
options: Leave level as it was (carryover)
Set level to null
Set level to dontcare
Reset the whole state
blocks.explain: Null and dontcare both remove the filter, but dontcare also records that the user answered the question. A system that later asks *which level?* would be asking something already answered. Carryover keeps the old filter, which is the wrong behavior here.

blocks.question: Location is a multi-valued list currently holding [US]. The user says *also Canada*. What should the new value be?
options: [Canada]
null
dontcare
[US, Canada]
blocks.explain: With a multi-valued slot, *also* adds to the list. [Canada] would be the result of *Canada instead*. The schema has to declare the slot multi-valued for this to work at all.

lessons.title: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries

blocks.md: Now run the whole toy session. The tracker (an LLM) reads the previous state and the new message and emits a **diff**: which slots to set, which to remove, and whether to reset. Plain code applies the diff, and a query builder turns the state into a search query. The LLM never writes the query directly.

Why a diff instead of the full state? SOM-DST measured this: TRADE generates a value for all 30 slots every turn, while SOM-DST generates values only for slots it decides to UPDATE, 1.14 on average per turn on MultiWOZ 2.1 test. A diff is shorter, every change is explicit and auditable, and carryover cannot go wrong because the model never retypes unchanged slots.

Function calling (tool use) is a natural way to get a diff out of an LLM. You declare a tool whose input is a JSON Schema, and the model returns a call with arguments matching it. Anthropic's API returns a `tool_use` block; setting `strict: true` on the tool makes sampling constrained to the schema. OpenAI's strict mode requires `additionalProperties: false` and every property in `required`, with optional fields written as a union with null, which is why the schema below uses null for *no change*.

blocks.caption: A diff tool. In set, null means no change for that slot; deletions go in remove, so the two meanings of null never collide.

blocks.md: Strict mode guarantees the diff is **schema-valid**, not that it is **right**. A perfectly typed `{"remove": []}` for *drop the salary limit* is still a wrong state. Schema enforcement removes parsing failures; only evaluation (lesson 6) catches meaning failures.

scenes.caption: T1 *Senior backend engineer jobs in the US, at least 150k*: four adds. Query: "backend engineer" AND level:senior AND location:US AND salary_min>=150000. 2 matches (J1, J2).
T2 *now only remote ones*: one add, four carryovers. Query gains AND remote:true. 1 match (J1). The message never mentions backend or the US; the state supplies them.
T3 *actually make it staff level*: one replace. Query has level:staff instead of level:senior. 2 matches (J4, J12).
T4 *drop the salary limit*: one remove. The salary clause disappears from the query. 3 matches (J4, J5, J12): J5 pays 135k and was hidden before.
T5 *start over: data engineer roles in Canada*: reset, then two adds. Query: "data engineer" AND location:Canada. 2 matches (J8, J9).

blocks.code:
T1  "backend engineer" AND level:senior AND location:US AND salary_min>=150000               matches: J1, J2
T2  "backend engineer" AND level:senior AND location:US AND remote:true AND salary_min>=150000 matches: J1
T3  "backend engineer" AND level:staff AND location:US AND remote:true AND salary_min>=150000  matches: J4, J12
T4  "backend engineer" AND level:staff AND location:US AND remote:true                          matches: J4, J5, J12
T5  "data engineer" AND location:Canada                                                          matches: J8, J9
blocks.caption: Generated queries and matches against the 12-posting toy index (computed by script).

blocks.title: Applying the T4 and T5 diffs

scenes.caption: T4 starts from the T3 state. dict(state) copies it, so every slot is carried over unless the diff says otherwise.
remove lists salary_min, so that slot becomes None. Nothing else changes.
to_query skips None slots, so the salary clause is simply absent.
scenes.output: "backend engineer" AND level:staff AND location:US AND remote:true

scenes.caption: T5 has reset=true: every slot is cleared before anything is set.
Then the two values from the message are added.
The new query carries nothing from the old search.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the tracker misses the reset at T5 and emits only *set role = data engineer, location = Canada*. What query runs, and how many of the 12 postings match?
blocks.reveal: Level staff and remote true are carried over from the old search, so the query is `"data engineer" AND level:staff AND location:Canada AND remote:true`, which matches **1** posting (J9) instead of 2. The user asked for a fresh search and got one silently narrowed by constraints from a search they abandoned.

blocks.md: Let the LLM decide **what changed**; let code decide **what the state is** and **what the query is**. This split makes carryover free, makes every change visible in logs, and turns the hardest part into a small, testable classification problem.

blocks.question: In the diff schema above, `set` uses null to mean *no change*. What goes wrong if you also used `set.salary_min = null` to mean *remove the salary limit*?
options: Nothing, the two meanings are the same
The schema becomes invalid in strict mode
apply_diff cannot tell *leave salary alone* from *delete salary*, so either every turn deletes it or no turn can
The query builder would crash on null
blocks.explain: One value cannot carry two meanings. Keeping removals in their own list (or using an explicit operation enum per slot, as SOM-DST does) keeps *no change* and *delete* distinguishable.

blocks.question: Which turn in the session is a replace rather than an add?
options: T2 now only remote ones
T3 actually make it staff level
T4 drop the salary limit
T1 the first search
blocks.explain: Level already held senior and changes to staff, so it is a replace. T2 fills a null slot (add), T4 empties a slot (remove), and T1 is four adds onto an empty state.

lessons.title: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown

blocks.md:
After T4 the assistant shows three jobs, sorted by salary:

1. J4, Umbrella, 190k
2. J12, Vandelay, 180k
3. J5, Hooli, 135k

The user replies *tell me more about the second one*, then *hide the Hooli one*, then *save those*. None of these words name a job. They point at **what the system showed**.

References in search sessions come in a few kinds:

- **Ordinal**: *the second one*, *the last one*. Needs the shown list in display order.
- **Attribute**: *the Hooli one*, *the remote one*. Needs the attributes of the shown items.
- **Set**: *those*, *these*. Needs the whole shown list.
- **Entity**: *that company*, *same team*. Needs the entity mentioned or shown most recently.

TREC CAsT shows why this matters for evaluation design. In 2019, organizers made later turns depend only on earlier user utterances, not on system responses, so topics stayed reusable. The biggest change in CAsT 2020 was that utterances refer to previous system responses, and the organizers had to supply a single **canonical response** per turn so every system was interpreted against the same shown content. Your system has the same problem: references are resolved against a specific response.

So the state needs a second part besides the filters: a **shown** record holding the ordered ids of the results on screen, tagged with the turn that produced them. The tracker sees this list with positions and attributes and outputs a reference such as *ordinal 2*; code maps it to an id.

scenes.caption: T4 runs as before. The app stores the filters and also the ordered ids shown: [J4, J12, J5] as shown list v4.
The app sends the message plus shown v4 with positions. The tracker returns a reference, not an id it typed itself. Code maps ordinal 2 to J12.
An attribute reference becomes a filter edit: add Hooli to an exclude_companies slot. The new results are J4 and J12, saved as shown v6.
*those* is a set reference. It resolves to the list on screen now, shown v6, so the app saves J4 and J12, not the three jobs from v4.

blocks.prompt: A developer resolves *the second one* by re-running the current query and taking result 2, instead of reading the stored shown list. In testing it works. What breaks in production?
blocks.reveal: Anything that changes the ranking between the two turns: a new posting is indexed, a job closes, a ranking model is updated, personalization differs, or the user changed the sort. Result 2 of a fresh run is then a different job from the one the user saw in position 2. References must resolve against the stored list the user actually saw, which is why that list is part of the state.

blocks.md: *those* has two readings that lead to different operations. In *save those* or *compare those*, it is a **set of ids**, frozen at the moment of the message. In *only those in Austin* it is a **constraint**: keep the current filters and add one. A useful test is whether the result should change if new postings arrive tomorrow. If yes, it is a filter; if no, it is a set of ids.

Do not ask the LLM to copy job ids out of text. Give it the shown list with positions and attributes and let it output a position or an attribute match; code does the lookup. A model that types ids can produce a well-formed id that was never shown.
References point at a response, not at the conversation. Store the ordered ids you displayed, with a version, and resolve ordinals, attributes and *those* against that stored list.

blocks.question: Shown list v4 is [J4, J12, J5]. The user says *hide the Hooli one*, and the assistant shows [J4, J12]. The user then says *open the second one*. Which job should open?
options: J5, because it was second in the original search
J12, because it is second in the list currently on screen
J12, because the tracker remembers it from the previous turn
Ask a clarifying question every time
blocks.explain: Ordinals refer to the most recent list the user saw, here shown v6 = [J4, J12]. J12 happens to be second in both lists, but the reason it is right is the current list; the third option names the right job for the wrong reason, and would fail if the lists differed.

blocks.question: Which use of *those* should become a filter edit rather than a frozen set of ids?
options: save those
email me those
only those that are remote
compare those
blocks.explain: *only those that are remote* narrows the search, and should keep working as postings change, so it is a constraint added to the filters. Saving, emailing and comparing act on the specific items on screen.

lessons.title: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing

blocks.md: Sometimes a message has more than one reasonable state update. After T3 the user has just set two slots, level (T3) and remote (T2). If they now say *drop that*, the tracker cannot know which one. The system can guess, or it can take the initiative and ask: *Drop the staff level or the remote filter?* A system that can ask is called **mixed-initiative**.

Aliannejadi et al. (SIGIR 2019) formalized asking clarifying questions in open-domain information-seeking conversations and built **Qulac**, over 10,000 question-answer pairs for 198 TREC topics with 762 facets. With an oracle that always picks the best question, asking just one question improved retrieval by over 170% in P@1. Gains were larger for ambiguous queries than for faceted ones, and larger for shorter queries. The oracle is an upper bound; the paper also shows real selected questions that lowered performance.

Asking is not free. The CIS survey frames it as a decision the system makes at every step: ask a clarifying question, or show results. In a ten-blue-links interface a user can skip a clarification, but in a speech-only or single-answer interface the question costs a full turn. TREC CAsT 2022 added a mixed-initiative subtask in which the system could ask a clarifying or follow-up question instead of answering.

A simple cost model makes the decision concrete. Let $p$ be the probability that your best interpretation is wrong, $C_w$ the cost of acting on a wrong interpretation, and $C_a$ the cost of one extra question. Guessing has expected cost $p\,C_w$; asking costs $C_a$.

blocks.caption: Simplified: it ignores that a question can itself be misunderstood and that asking too often annoys users. Research systems learn this policy instead of fixing costs.

blocks.title: Expected cost of guessing vs asking

x.label: p (chance the best guess is wrong)

scenes.caption: With Ca = 0.3 and Cw = 1, the lines cross at p = 0.3. Below it guessing is cheaper on average; above it, asking is.
A wrong guess that is cheap to undo (say an extra result the user can ignore, Cw = 0.4) pushes the threshold to 0.75. Guess and show the interpretation.
A wrong guess that is expensive (a reset that throws away a long session, Cw = 1.2) lowers the threshold to 0.25. Ask sooner.

blocks.md: Apply it to the session. At T2, *now only remote ones* after *in the US* has two readings: remote jobs open to US candidates (keep location) or remote jobs anywhere (drop location). In the toy index the first gives 1 match (J1) and the second gives 2 (J1, J7). A wrong guess costs one extra or one missing posting and is easy to see and fix, so guess the more literal reading and keep location.

blocks.prompt: After T3 the user says *drop that*. Both level and remote were set in the last two turns. Should the system guess or ask, by the cost model?
blocks.reveal: Ask. There are two nearly equally likely readings, so $p$ is close to 0.5, and a wrong guess removes a filter the user wanted while keeping the one they wanted gone; they may not notice which. With any asking cost below about half the cost of a wrong guess, asking wins. A short question listing the two options (*the staff level or the remote filter?*) costs one turn and fully resolves it.

blocks.md: Show the state as editable chips (backend engineer, staff, US, remote) next to the results. The user can see your interpretation and fix a wrong guess in one click. This lowers the cost of a wrong guess, which by the cost model lets you ask less often.
Do not ask about what the state already answers, or about slots marked dontcare. Repeated or redundant questions are the fastest way to make mixed-initiative feel worse than a plain search box.
Ask when the readings are close in probability and a wrong guess is costly or hard to notice. Otherwise, guess the most literal reading, act on it, and make the interpretation visible.

blocks.question: Your system asks a clarifying question whenever the tracker's top reading has confidence below 0.9. Users complain it asks too much. Using the cost model, what is the principled fix?
options: Raise the confidence threshold to 0.99
Never ask clarifying questions
Set the threshold per situation from the cost ratio: ask only when the chance of being wrong exceeds Ca / Cw, and lower Cw by showing editable filter chips
Ask two questions at once so the conversation is shorter
blocks.explain: A fixed confidence cutoff ignores how costly a wrong guess is. The threshold should be Ca / Cw, which is high when mistakes are cheap and visible. Raising the cutoff to 0.99 makes the system ask even more.

blocks.question: In Qulac, which kind of query benefited more from clarification?
options: Ambiguous queries, more than faceted ones
Long, very specific queries
Faceted queries, more than ambiguous ones
Neither; clarification helped all queries equally
blocks.explain: Aliannejadi et al. found larger improvements for ambiguous topics than for faceted ones, and a negative correlation between query length and the best question's gain, so shorter queries need clarification more often.

lessons.title: Storing state server-side and measuring it

blocks.md:
Where does the state live between turns? Two designs:

- **Re-derive**: store only the transcript. Each turn, the model reads the history and outputs the **full** state. TRADE works like this: it encodes the recent dialogue history and generates a value for every slot every turn.
- **Stored state**: keep the state object on the server, keyed by session. Each turn, the model reads the previous state plus the latest turns and outputs a **diff**. SOM-DST works like this: its input is the previous turn, the current turn and the previous state, used as an explicit memory.

scenes.caption: Re-derive: stateless servers and self-healing (a mistake can be fixed next turn by re-reading), but input grows with every turn and every slot is regenerated, so an untouched slot can flip.
Stored: input stays small, only changed slots are produced, and UI actions (clicking a chip to remove a filter) update the state directly. But a wrong state persists until something corrects it.

blocks.md: Two practical points decide most real systems. First, users edit filters by **clicking**, not only by typing, and those edits are not in the chat transcript. A re-derive design must write UI events into the history, or the next turn will undo them. Second, stored state makes errors persistent. The common compromise is to store the state **and** an append-only event log of diffs and UI events per session, so you can replay, audit, and re-derive when you change the tracker.

Version the state (turn number or counter) and send the version with each request. If two requests race, for example a chip click and a typed message, the server can reject the stale one instead of silently merging.

Evaluation measures the state directly, per turn. The TRADE paper reports the two standard metrics, defined as follows. **Joint goal accuracy (JGA)**: a turn counts as correct only if every slot in the predicted state matches the gold state exactly. **Slot accuracy**: each slot is compared to its gold value separately, and the score is the fraction that match.

blocks.caption: T turns, J slots, B the full state, V a single slot value. Hats are predictions.

blocks.title: Per-slot correctness of two trackers on the toy session

scenes.caption: Tracker A reads *now only remote ones* as dropping location. The error is carried over until the reset at T5. Slot accuracy 22/25 = 0.88; JGA 2/5 = 0.40.
Tracker B gets T2 right but misses the delete at T4, keeping salary_min = 150000. Slot accuracy 24/25 = 0.96; JGA 4/5 = 0.80.

blocks.prompt: Tracker A's location error at T3 and T4 does not change the results at all (both give the same jobs as the gold state). Only T2 shows a wrong job (J7, a Canadian posting). If you evaluated only retrieval quality per turn, what would you conclude about tracker A, and why is that misleading?
blocks.reveal: Retrieval would look wrong only at T2 and perfect at T3 and T4, because the toy index has no non-US staff remote backend jobs. The state is still wrong on three turns, and the bug will surface as soon as such a posting exists. State metrics catch latent errors that end-to-end metrics hide; report both.

blocks.md: Slot accuracy is easy to inflate because most slots on most turns are null and simply carried over. TRADE on MultiWOZ reports 96.92% slot accuracy but 48.62% joint goal accuracy across 30 slots. As a rough sanity check, if each slot were right independently with probability $a$, joint accuracy would be $a^J$; with $a = 0.9692$ and $J = 30$ that gives about 0.39. Real errors are correlated, so the measured 0.4862 is higher, but the lesson holds: JGA is the honest headline number.

blocks.title: Joint accuracy if slot errors were independent

scenes.caption: With 30 slots, a = 0.9692 gives about 0.39 under independence. TRADE's measured JGA (0.4862) sits above the curve because real slot errors cluster in the same turns.
With 5 slots, like the toy schema, the same per-slot accuracy gives about 0.86. Bigger schemas make joint accuracy much harder to achieve.

blocks.md: Build your own evaluation set from real sessions: gold state after every turn, written by annotators. Report JGA, per-slot accuracy, and per-operation precision and recall, with deletes and resets broken out. Expect label noise: MultiWOZ 2.1 re-annotated the original data and changed over 32% of state annotations across 40% of dialogue turns, so double-annotate a sample and measure agreement before trusting small differences.
Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

blocks.question: Tracker X has 99% slot accuracy and 60% JGA. Tracker Y has 97% slot accuracy and 70% JGA, on the same data. Which better reflects how often a user sees a fully correct search?
options: X, because slot accuracy is higher
Y, because JGA counts a turn correct only when every slot is right, which is what the user experiences
They are equivalent
Neither metric relates to user experience
blocks.explain: One wrong slot makes the whole search wrong for the user. JGA measures exactly that. X's errors are spread across more turns, so although each slot is usually right, fewer complete states are.

blocks.question: Your app stores only the chat transcript and re-derives state each turn. A user removes the remote filter by clicking its chip, then types *show staff roles too*. What is the likely bug?

Joint goal accuracy cannot be computed
There is no bug; re-derivation handles UI edits automatically
blocks.explain: UI edits are not in the transcript unless you write them there. Re-deriving from text alone resurrects the removed filter. Either log UI events into the history or keep server-side state that the click updates directly.
